Can we put our hands together for her? Can we also have Teresia Kigundu of Women Live Health, Madam Daphne Chamambo, Chief Nurse and Midwifery Officer of Zambia, Professor Doreen Kaura of the Pan-African Midwifery Alliance, Madam Laurence Bontero of FASFA, Dr. Art Garissi who is an independent expert by representing UNFPA ASTRO. Part A will set the agenda with global competencies and importance of regional coalitions for power and influence, whilst part B will give us deep dive into facilitative and promotive actions to be taken so that we can organize, we can institutionalize and we can influence our profession within the Africa milieu. There will be three speakers for the part A and then all of them and then in part B our four remaining speakers will speak to specific questions and then all of them would address some general questions that we believe would be of use to all of us. On that note, without much ado, I'd like to call Professor Jacqueline Dunkley-Bent to give us her five minutes speaking points.
Thank you. Thank you, Dr. Jemima and the five minutes starts now. So I'm delighted to be here to speak to you.

Sorry? I'm delighted to be here and to speak to you about midwifery leadership, global midwifery leadership, and I'm really excited to be amongst such powerful, powerful, strong midwife leaders. Stand tall because your voices matter. So we're going to go on a little five minute journey.

Here we go. So I just want to share with you the key to achieving government policy ambitions. We are turning global commitments into country-owned priorities and the only way to do that is to have technical, technical presence and that's you.

You have the authority. A very short, actually a very long time ago, a mentor of mine, a baroness, said to me when I was going into my first meeting in country with the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care, she said to me, you're going into that room for the first time. She was about 82 years old at the time and she's a member of the House of Lords and she said to me, you're going into that room for the first time.
Remember who the midwife is. It's you. Remember you have the authority.
Remember you have all these years of experience to tell them what they don't know. They don't know what you know. Go in and make a difference and that made all the difference to me.
So I commend this to you. You go and tell the world about who midwives are and what midwives stand for. So in going into global commitments, serve as authoritative policy voices.
You have the voice. You're not only clinical, you are a policy voice, a strategic actor. Align the whole system, not just clinical standards.

When you're advocating, don't just talk about midwifery education. That is weak if you don't talk about midwifery regulation and that's weak if you don't talk about gender equality and that's weak if you don't talk about your midwives associations. For the presidents in the room, you count, we count and together we can.
There's more on the slide here. We haven't got time. We need to.

How do they support? How do you support? How do we support achieving government policy ambitions? You can see on the screen here but what I would say to you is when there's a global policy ambition, what do you do in country? Does it sit on a shelf and gather dust or do you translate that into what this means for my country? To do that you need to ask some critical questions about your country. What are the pressing challenges for maternal and newborn health? How can this global policy difference make a difference locally and how will this impact on the lives of women and newborns? You bridge the gap between the global and the bedside. You have the authority to do this because of your experience.

I'm going to canter through these. How can governments enable and empower midwife leaders? Well you can see on the screen here but just paraphrasing a little, we need to support midwifery leadership in terms of education. Let's empower and support each other.
Let's not eat our young. Let's develop our young and support each other. We need to commit to adhering to the global competencies for midwife leaders.

I'm really proud of those competencies not just because I led the development with many of you but these are meaningful for all of you at country level and I'll be sharing more about these tomorrow in the leadership session and I cannot leave this slide without mentioning create a national chief midwife role and ICM are in the business, my last slide, of helping you to make those changes from global to bedside. So we have a position statement that was signed off by council this year on how to develop a chief midwife role but we didn't stop there, we wanted to establish a policy brief for you. So it's not just about the guidance, it's about how do I communicate, what's my elevator pitch in relation to a chief midwife, it's in this document.

Policy leads, perm secs, health secretaries, presidents, governments, why do we need a chief midwife? It's in this document. What will one do? It's in this document. What will be the impact on the lives of women and newborns? It's in this document.

Thank you so much for listening. Thank you so much. Give it to her again for being in time and thanks for the insights concerning the fact that we have to be our own advocates and it starts as a round table discussion.

Thank you so much. Our next presenter is from Women Health Lift and she is going to give us insights around building strong midwifery coalitions for policy influence. Let's put our hands together for her.
Good morning everyone. Good morning. I'm so excited to be here.
You can call me Terry. I'm sure that will click home better. Yeah.

This is some bit of a brief conversation that I want to talk about this morning. Building strong midwifery coalitions for policy influence. Professor already told us how important we are and the importance of influencing as we work alongside different other people.

My key message this morning then, how do we influence so that we are able to talk to everyone who needs to be part of the conversations that we are having? How do we ensure that they are hearing us, they are listening to us in addition to influencing policies and structures and systems because that is where the biggest work always lies. So this is just a little about Women Lift Health. Please read a little more on our websites and social so that you get to hear exactly who we are.
But Women Lift Health works with women leaders embedded in health institutions across Africa. We are also in South Asia and North America. Our key business is to build their power and influence.

That is very core. So building your power and influence so that then we can be able to shape what is happening in decisions, not just to be on the table but to partake what is happening on that table. Leadership is not a possession.
Please let's hear that. It's not a possession. It is a practice.
And a key simple question here this morning, who holds formal leadership in this hall this morning? Just raise your hand quickly. Who is in a formal leadership role here? I see hands up. Good.

Who has changed a mind or a practice in the last one month? Great. So what does that tell us? We are all leaders. You are not in leadership because of the position that you hold but you are already leading in whatever it is that you're doing.
So everyone seated here, me and you, we are all leaders and that's the denominator. No single voice moves policies. That's very important.

We have been here this week and will continue to be here the rest of today. But if we have no coordinated voice and we are not coming together as coalitions and groups speaking one mind, there isn't so much we can be able to do. So we need, I love that quote and it's the only quote I'm reading on the this slide.

We cannot address decision makers with a hundred fragmented voices. We need to build a common voice to do what? To influence structural and policy change. That's why coalition building is very important.

But within those coalitions, then we need to speak one voice so that we can be able to move the needles in the direction in which they need to move. Shifting the system, very important. So it's not just the practice, it's also influencing the systems and the structures so that as we midwives come in, then we have a conducive environment where systems and structures can allow us now to use up our power and influence.

Lead up, across and out because that is what we do. You love to manage up, influence upwards. You have to influence across and you have to go out there, talk to partners, communities, groups, media, wherever that would be.

So our influence is not just within the groups that we are in as midwives, it will go up across and outside the space that you're too familiar with. This is a simple way of influencing that. Use the hand, evidence and data.

Do we have that? Are we compiling this data? Are we communicating this data? Are we creating stories, documenting stories and sharing these stories with the world? Then the last one is the hands, a practical ask. What, who, how and when? And lastly, your coalition starts with one ally. Bring as many midwives as possible to the coalitions so that we grow.

And once we grow, then we'll be enhancing our power and influence to be able to move the needles in the right direction. So thank you very much and looking forward to having more conversation on influence tomorrow for those who will be attending the workshop. Bye-bye.

Thank you so much, Terry, for letting us know that leadership is not a position, it is a practice and an influence. Thank you so much. We'll continue with our speaker positioning by inviting Professor Doreen to give us how can regional networks such as yours translate solidarity and collaboration into coordinated advocacy, shared learning and stronger national midwifery institutions.
Five minutes. Thank you. Thank you, Amanda, moderator.

And I'm just following through to what the previous speakers have just alluded to. I begin by asking ourselves this fundamental question. What is the purpose of solidarity if it does not translate to power, to influence, to structures, to support one another in action to change the conditions in the midwives work? We just heard that 100 fragmented organizations do not have power.

Thus, I speak about the Pan-African Midwives Alliance. What is the Pan-African Midwives Alliance? It is a collective voice for African midwives. It is an opportunity to move African midwifery from fragmented voices to collective influence where we amplify voices through policies, strategy and decision making.

It is an opportunity to create continental platform through which national midwives associations are strengthened and voices amplified. We want to complement the work of existing international, national, regional and global organizations. We are not competing.
We are complementing. We want to help adapt global maternal and neonatal health and midwifery priorities to national realities and context. We want to bring this to our villages through PAMA.

So, a mandate from African midwives started with a dream on 30th May 2024 in Accra, Ghana, where we had 120 participants hailing from 27 countries. The resolution from that was to establish a continental midwifery entity to serve as a unified voice and driving force for midwifery in Africa and represent these midwives. If you look at the logo, it tells you that Africa is a sunshine that we want to keep.
So, the summit was well represented. These are some of the pictures of that summit. And what PAMA aims to contribute is continental representation of advocacy, collaboration and partnership.

And I must emphasize collaboration and partnership, leadership and professional development, knowledge exchange, research promotion, midwifery visibility and mentorship. And solidarity begins with an individual joining, an organization joining, international organizations joining, so that we have a voice for Africa. During our progress, we established a constitution and we have adopted the constitution.
We were supported by UNFPA. It's translated in French. Portuguese.

And it will be adopted on 30th November in our General Assembly. It's formally registered in South Africa. And we also have a steering committee that has been spending sleepless nights to make sure that midwives speak as one voice.
Our next phase and opportunity is to raise awareness, membership recruitment and engagement. And we are open to individuals and organizations. Virtual secretariat arrangements are in place.
Resource mobilization is ongoing. And stakeholder engagement and collaboration. That is the website which we are launching.
We're saying this and I'm saying this slowly. Africa is about Ubuntu, Untu, Antu, Bantu. It reminds us that we are because we are together.
But professional solidarity, being together must also mean acting together. That I believe is an opportunity and responsibility for PAMA. Join us so that we can have one concerted voice.
We are Africans. And again I repeat, say after me, Africa will no longer be a dark continent with me in it. Somebody repeat that? You are the sunshine of Africa.
And we are going to make those footprints if we join hands together. Thank you. Now coalitions and what they can do to translate solidarity and collaboration.
We now move into our panel discussions. And I am excited to start with Madam Daphne Chamambo from Zambia. Madam Daphne, you have two minutes.

How can government institutionalize midwifery and ensure midwives influence national health policy planning and resource allocation? Thank you very much. I'm told under two minutes. First of all, I want to say that we need to realize that midwives are not just providers of a service, but they are also supposed to be major contributors in terms of planning and also decision making in our health sector.

So number one, there's need for institutionalizing midwifery leadership. We need to establish the midwifery structures in our national level, provincial or regional or sub-district, depending on your country. And this can happen through collaboration with the associations, the registrators and academia.
That's what we did in Zambia. Our court advocated for that. And as I'm talking, we have a full-fledged directorate of nursing and midwifery.

And also once you do that, now you have a way through to be involved in policy and planning. It's very, very important. It's high time we started being involved in policy and planning, because there's no way you can let someone plan for you.

You need to plan yourselves. And once you have done that, even leadership, the government will come to realize to say, oh, so midwives are able to plan. You need to take your seat and join during the planning meetings.

Leadership development. As midwives, we have not to sit down. We have to build ourselves every day so that we are up to date, because we need to have a strengthened leadership in terms of management, police analysis, and even being advocates for skilled midwives to take it up.
Thank you. Thank you so much, Madam Daphne, for that, helping us to know that midwives have a responsibility at the national level. Madam Montero, it's your turn.

Can you let us know how regional networks can translate solidarity and collaboration within the French milieu, coordinated advocacy, and shared learning as based on experience from FASFA? Thank you. Thank you, Madam Daphne. Thank you.

Thank you so much, Madam Montero, for letting us know the work that FASFA is doing and some of the expectations of the regional network. Thank you. At this point, we would continue, and I'm happy to call upon Dr. Gerisi, who would tell us also their perspective using the Tunisian Midwives Association.

Thank you, Jemima. I will answer to your question not on behalf of the Tunisian Association of Midwives, but based on my experience, my privilege, to have provided technical assistance and mentorship to three regional midwifery networks, one for the ex-FASFA co, actually FASFAF, one to a regional midwifery network for midwifery associations in the MENA region, Middle East and North Africa, and the actual AHMAC, Arab Regional Midwifery Advisory Group. So based on these three experiences, I would highlight three points.

The first one, when we talk about Africa, we talk about one continent, but in reality, there is a huge diversity in terms of languages, religions, cultural practices, even also the states of midwifery. The commonality is the medical model of care, and so we need tailored midwifery networks. That's why we have an advisory group in the Eastern Mediterranean region.

The second point, my philosophical side, is to say that we inspire, we only give what we have. We inspire by who we are, by how we behave, not by what we say, what we know, and what we do. So that means I'm calling the networks to be a role model.

And the third point, the importance for networks is to gather selected champions, and we do have champions, and also potential leaders. Leadership is a readiness. You look, you watch children playing together, and you see that one of them is leading the group, potential future leader.

So they have to be humble, and humility is not in our cultural vocabulary in the region. So we need to learn to be humble, to develop the sense of self-questioning, self-assessment, self-awareness. It is a constant work on the self, to develop self-confidence, self-esteem, transcend the ego, develop the sense of volunteer work and dedication, and develop the sense, it is very much missing, of sisterhood.
So this is what I wanted to highlight. Thank you. Thank you so much, Dr. Art, for giving us this insight.

We know that leadership, even in childhood, there is a potential, and we need to harness that. Now, Ibrahim, Yime, Ibrahim, how can professional associations become stronger advocacy institutions that mobilize members and influence governments and health systems decisions? Two minutes. Okay, thank you very much for the opportunity.

I would like to speak a little bit about the Ethiopian Midwifery Association. We are a 34-year-old professional association, having 35 staff, and also representing 27,000 midwives in the country. And we work with the Ministry of Health, government, other government agencies, academic institutes.

So how we become strong advocates of the midwifery agenda in the country? Because we build institutional credibility, having an executive board, and also the secretariat having its own roles in the country. So we always implement organizational capacity assessments, and also accountability systems, and also we take actions from the organizational assessment, so that we just implement improvement strategies. For example, the micro-assessment with the NIPID, OSCAR assessment, with the PAYAGO-MACAT assessment, we all implement this organizational assessment strategies and implement improvement strategies.

With this, for example, we have been leading a consortium of professional associations, more than 15, to respond to the COVID-19 pandemic, and also institutionalizing the continuing professional development in the country, and also in the development of health workforce, compassionate and respectful health workforce in the country. Receiving grants, large grants from the Ministry of Health, and also sub-granting to other health professionals. This is one of the strategies we advocate.

And the second is we translate evidence into policy, through doing research, and also converting into policy briefs, submitting to the Ministry of Health. For example, if I tell you one story of ours, it's a clinical midwife story, which are trained to provide CMOC services in the remote community. This was initially provided for health officers and nurses only, then we came in and developed curriculums and also provide this training for midwives.

Now, Regional Health Bureau, the Ministry of Health is also supporting education and deployment of midwives in the remote facilities. Thank you so much. Thank you for letting us know what Ethiopia Midwives Association has been able to do to represent power and influence.
Wonderful, wonderful. Now, we move on to a general question for all of you, and it will be one minute, precisely, one minute. I'd like to start from Dr. Atif.

What practical mechanism can ensure that midwives at the front line have a voice in national, regional, and global decision-making? One minute. Thank you for the question, Jemima. Again, I will base my answer on my experience in Yemen, and a story I would share with you, a success story, and I'm talking about community midwives.

I went to Yemen in 2010, and I had to go to Aden. Aden is in the south. And you went to the villages, and one officer at the municipality told me, we love our community midwife, and we want to keep her.
And her husband is a soldier, and he received an order of transfer to Sana'a, to the capital. But the community didn't want to leave the midwife. She has to follow her husband.

So the community leaders gathered and went to Sana'a, to the capital, to meet the president of the republic, saying, we want to keep the midwife in our community, so I will ask you, please, to cancel the order of transfer. And he canceled the order of transfer, and they kept the midwife. Wow.

Thank you so much. So it tells us the power of community, and what they can do to transform systems. Madam Ontario, how can government and professional leadership reinforce each other? Thank you, Madam.

I believe that government and professional leadership of midwives is not the training of midwives, specialists, and midwives at the decision-making level. It is in collaboration with schools. The government allows midwives to review the different clinics in the country.

And today, which is a great achievement for Benin, usually, when we recruit 100 midwives, we can recruit 300 or 500 midwives. It is the opposite today. In Benin, the government has recruited 100 midwives for 300 midwives.

So that means that the government recognizes the priority work of midwives in Benin. And also, when midwives have solid arguments to present in front of the government, the government finishes accepting what we demand. Thank you.
Wow. Wow. Wow.
This is the power of advocacy. Thank you. Now we come to the issue of power and representation.

Ibrahim, are midwives adequately represented in the institutions where decisions about health financing, workforce planning, education, and service delivery are made? And why? No, Jemima. Unfortunately, midwives are not adequately represented. For example, when you see the case of Ethiopia, we have only 3% of the 27 midwives having leadership positions.

And the Minister of Health in the regional health bureau, this is a very challenge that we are facing. So we need to support them in preparing leadership programs and also support having a space for the leadership programs. Otherwise, we cannot influence in the ministry.

There is an adage that says, if you are not in the table, you are the menu. So other professionals will discuss on the agenda of midwives while midwives are not in the position. So we need to be there.
We need to advocate for midwives to have positions in the ministry. Thank you. Thank you.

Wumben Lifts, how do we establish governance arrangements that ensure representation, transparency, accountability, and meaningful participation in decision making? Thank you, Jemima, for that. I think I appreciate the representation as one of the panelists, my colleagues have mentioned. And I want us to move also, once we get the representation at the table, do we have the voice to influence the policies and the decisions? So yes, let's have the light structures. Let's have the light governance, the light systems. Let's also encourage and build the capacities of the midwives so that once we get represented, then we are also able to use our voice and power to be able to influence.
Powerful. Powerful. Thank you.

So as we want to claim power, we have to prepare ourselves in our bedrooms, because we cannot just send somebody, anybody to sit at the table. We need to prepare ourselves, and that is capacity building. Jacqueline, what governance mechanism should exist between global bodies, regional networks, national associations, and government structures to ensure that commitments translate into action? From the evidence and from personal experience, global commitments fail because accountability structures are weak.

It's really important that when we have a global strategy and it's contextualized at country level, there is a funded implementation plan that is a part of the health system plan for sustainability. We need to stop thinking that the crumbs that we receive to improve lives will last for decades. We have a responsibility to do something about it.

Funded implementation plans and then local action plans. But even with local action plans from experience, our people need to understand what these global commitments mean, what it means to them, their ownership, and what it will mean to their practice, to women and newborns. But it's important also to understand and have the accountability for the actors, the actors who are shaping this global commitment into a country context, the actors who are responsible and accountable for taking this to a local level.

So the actors are really important. And then the killer question, there needs to be line of sight from ministry, country ministry, region, local. What difference is this making to women, newborns, and their families? There is no point in having an amazing commitment that does nothing to those on the ground.
And there's no point in having a commitment that lasts for a day or a month. Thank you so much, Jackie. Commitments must transcend into observable impacts on the mother and the newborn.

Doreen, how do we ensure that regional and global commitments translate into tangible improvements in national policies, professional practice, and working conditions of midwives? Thank you. Thank you. Every morning when the antelope wakes up, it has to run, run faster than the fastest lion in order to survive.

In Africa, we have a lot of lions. And what I'm saying is that we have a lot of global commitment, fantastic innovations from ICM, from UNFPA, from FAFSA, from all these other organizations. How do we translate it so that we survive with all these lions that are running around us? It means that we need commitment, we need collaboration, we need consolidation, we need solidarity between all of us.

So PAMA is looking into engaging with all these other organizations in order for us to be able to translate that into mouthful bites from the bigger elephant. And the reason I'm saying that is when we get to hear from UNFPA or from ICM or from these other organizations, we hear a lot of these things. But how are we translating it to the ground? How do I get it to the village so that my mother gets to hear about menopause? How do we get it into the village so that my sister, my cousin, gets to hear about family planning? It is a difficult journey, but we can only do it if we have solidarity with consolidated planning, consolidated policies that are seeping down to the ground.
Thank you. Thank you so much. Thank you so much.

As we round off, Daphne and I would like you to give us one concrete way forward. What is one concrete commitment each level of leadership should make to strengthen midwifery leadership, coalitions, and governance over the next three years? Thank you very much. We need now to prioritize midwifery, not just midwives as providers, but we need to recognize importance and midwives should deliberate, empowering them to deliberate.

One word, not statements. You know, it's difficult, but we professional associations. Professional associations, thank you.

Voice in policy. Representation, power, and influence. Thank you.
